messages.subject: Besag/BYM including observations without neighbours
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to fit a model to areal data (property-level observations) and wish to account for spatial autocorrelation, which I have opted to do with a 'bym2' term. Due to the nature of the properties I am analysing, very few have shared boundaries, but many of them are within very close proximity of eachother (just not contiguous). Therefore, I've created a distance matrix containing the pair wise minimum distances between all properties, and have binarised this matrix based on a series of candidate thresholds (e.g., 100m, 250m, 500m and so on), where properties are considered neighbours (1 value in the binarised matrix) if they are less than x metres apart.

My issue arises due to the fact that under this methodology, some observations (properties) do not have any neighbours. I have been using spdep to convert the distance matrix to a 'nb' list and then trying to use the 'nb2INLA' function to convert this to an INLA-readable graph file - however, the function gives the error 'Error in card(nb) : zero length neighbour vector'. To my understanding, the 'besag'/'bym' models implemented in INLA can deal with observations not having any neighbours, but I'm wondering if there are any special steps I need to take to create a suitable graph file in these circumstances? And do I need to add any additional specifications to the bym2 random effect call? At the moment I am just using:

f(ID, model = 'bym2', scale.model = T, constr = T, graph = my_graph)

and have got the model to run succesfully when using an adjacency matrix based on k-nearest neighbours (so each observation always has at least 1 neighbour).

Thanks for any help,

Ciar

messages.body_plain:
I think what you do is fine. the cost of adding more data is linear in number of
data

maybe you do not need to set seed and num.threads as its runs better without:

On Sun, 2024-07-28 at 12:24 -0700, John Molitor wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm trying to estimate the Relative Risk (RR) from a logistic model. In the
> frequentist realm one often instead fits a Poisson model to binary data and
> then then fixes up the obvious model misspecification using a sandwich
> estimator. However, with Bayesian MCMC one can directly estimate the RR from a
> logistic model. (See:
> https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259486968_Using_Bayesian_Logistic_Regression_to_Estimate_the_Risk_or_Prevalence_Ratio
> )
>
> I can successfully implement the approach in the above cited paper via INLA,
> however I end up creating a dummy dataset of triple the size of the original.
> This approach works, but I wonder if there is a more efficient way to do this.
>
> Thanks,
>
> John
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> library(tidyverse)
> library(MASS)
>
> ## Here's the paper
> ###
> https://www.researchgate.net/publication/259486968_Using_Bayesian_Logistic_Regression_to_Estimate_the_Risk_or_Prevalence_Ratio
>
> ##########################
> ### Simulate some data ###
> ##########################
>
> set.seed(123)
> n <- 1000
> x1 <- rnorm(n)
> x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
> eta <- 0.5 + 0.5 * x1 - 1.5 * x2
> y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta))
>
> ###########################################
> ### Fit robust Poisson regression model ###
> ###########################################
>
> library(sandwich)
> library(lmtest)
> model <- glm(y ~ 1 + x1 + x2, family = poisson(link = "log"))
> summary(model)
> ct <- coeftest(model,vcov=sandwich)
>
> ct.est <- ct["x2","Estimate"]
> ct.error <- ct["x2","Std. Error"]
> ct.ci <http://ct.ci> <- exp(ct.est + c(-1,1) * 1.96 * ct.error)
>
> ###################################
> ### Fit Bayesian logistic model ###
> ###################################
>
> library(brms)
>
> dat <- tibble(y,x1,x2)
> m.bayes <- brm(
>     y ~ x1 + x2,
>     family = bernoulli(),
>     data=dat
> )
> mat <- as_tibble(m.bayes)
>
> dat.0 <- dat %>%
>     mutate(x2=0)
> dat.1 <- dat %>%
>     mutate(x2=1)
> dat.pred <- rbind(dat.0,dat.1)
>
> pl <- posterior_linpred(m.bayes,newdata=dat.pred)
>
> mf <- function(vec.org <http://vec.org>) {
>     vec <- plogis(vec.org <http://vec.org>)
>     bot <- mean(vec[1:n])
>     top <- mean(vec[n+1:n])
>     res <- top / bot
> }
> rr <- apply(pl,1,mf)
> median(rr)
> quantile(rr,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))
>
> ############
> ### INLA ###
> ############
>
> library(INLA)
>
> dat.pred.inla <- dat.pred %>%
>     mutate(y = NA)
> dat.inla <- rbind(dat,dat.pred.inla)
>
> m.inla <- inla(
>     y ~ x1 + x2,
>     family = "binomial",
>     control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
>     control.predictor=list(link=1),
>     data=dat.inla
> )
>
> get.samp <- function(mod,M=1000,seed=1,num.threads="1:1") {
>     samp <- inla.posterior.sample(M,mod,seed=seed,num.threads=num.threads)
>     latents <- t(sapply(samp,function(x) x$latent[,1]))
> }
> samp <- get.samp(m.inla,M=10000)
> pl.inla <- cbind(samp[,n + 1:n],samp[,2*n+1:n])
> rr.inla <- apply(pl.inla,1,mf)
> quantile(rr.inla,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))
